title: What is a binary search tree (BST): a binary tree where left child < parent < right child; this makes searching fast.
shortTitle: What is a Binary Search Tree (BST)?
keyPoints: BST ordering invariant: all left-subtree values are smaller, all right-subtree values are larger
Search, insert, and delete run in O(h) time where h is the tree height
Inorder traversal of a BST visits values in sorted ascending order
A degenerate BST (all one-sided) becomes a linked list with O(n) operations
Self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black) guarantee O(log n) height
Java's TreeMap and TreeSet are red-black BSTs providing sorted iteration and O(log n) operations

s1_definition.oneliner: A BST keeps smaller values on the left and larger on the right, so each comparison halves the search.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Binary Search Tree (BST)** – a binary tree that maintains an ordering invariant: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger.
- **Logarithmic search** – each comparison eliminates half the remaining tree, giving O(log n) search when the tree is balanced.
- **Inorder traversal** – visiting left, node, right produces values in sorted ascending order.
- **Self-balancing** – AVL and Red-Black trees keep the height logarithmic, preventing degeneration to a linked list.
- **Java standard library** – TreeMap and TreeSet are Red-Black BSTs providing sorted iteration and O(log n) operations.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India arranges account balances on a special noticeboard shaped like a tree. Every balance smaller than the one in your hand hangs on the left branch, and every larger balance hangs on the right. To find a particular balance you start at the top and at each step go left if smaller or right if larger. You never look at the whole board: you eliminate half the possibilities at every step.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  BST with account balances:

         50000
        /     \
     30000   70000
    /    \
  20000  40000

  Search for 40000:
  50000 → 40000 < 50000 → go left
  30000 → 40000 > 30000 → go right
  40000 → found! (3 comparisons)

  Inorder traversal:
  20000 → 30000 → 40000 → 50000 → 70000
  (sorted ascending)

  Degenerate BST (sorted inserts):
  10000
      \
     20000
         \
        30000
            \
           40000 → linked list, O(n) search
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A binary search tree maintains the ordering invariant that for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger. That single invariant makes searching fast: at each node you compare your target with the node's value and move left or right, discarding half the remaining tree on every step. In a balanced tree this gives O(log n) search, insert, and delete.

Inorder traversal of a BST visits values in sorted ascending order, which makes it a natural ordered map or ordered set. In the banking context, this means you can iterate account balances in sorted order and perform range queries like finding all balances between two amounts.

The danger is degeneration. If you insert sorted data into a naive BST, it becomes a linked list and operations fall back to O(n). Self-balancing trees like AVL and Red-Black fix this by rotating nodes to keep the height logarithmic. In production, use Java's TreeMap and TreeSet, which are Red-Black BSTs with guaranteed O(log n) operations.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh uses TreeMap to look up interest-rate tiers by balance. The floorEntry method finds the correct tier in O(log n), and sorted iteration lets the report list all tiers in ascending balance order without a separate sort.

Remember one sentence: a BST keeps smaller values left and larger values right, so each comparison halves the search space, and self-balancing variants guarantee that halving always works.
